chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Al-Minqari, from Al-Fudayl ibn Ayaz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The believer envies (in a good way) but does not envy (in a bad way), and the hypocrite envies (in a bad way) but does not envy (in a good way).

key_terms.يَحْسُدُ: To envy in a bad way (desiring the removal of a blessing from the other)
key_terms.يَغْبِطُ: To envy in a good way (desiring a blessing without wanting it removed from the other)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Ghabt and Hasad in Shia ethics?
ai.summary: This concise hadith from al-Kafi delineates the spiritual psychology of the believer versus the hypocrite by contrasting 'ghabṭ' (non-malicious desire for blessings) with 'ḥasad' (malicious desire for deprivation). In Shia scholarly tradition, this distinction highlights that the believer’s envy is a form of healthy aspiration that coexists with gratitude, whereas the hypocrite’s envy is rooted in spiritual deficiency and a desire to see others diminished. This classification serves as a practical diagnostic tool for self-reflection on the purity of one's inner intentions regarding worldly and divine favors.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Al Qasim Bin Muhammad, from Al Minqary, from Al Fuzayl Bin Ayaaz, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘A Momin backbites but does not envy, and the hypocrite envies and does not backbite’.
en.sarwar: 7. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from al-Minqari from al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyad from abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) who has said the following: “
A believer asks Allah for help but does not envy, and a hypocrite envies, but does not ask Allah for help.”
